items.title: CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall
items.summary:
US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson . The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project's inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

"The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living," said Jackson-based CLB Architects .

The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

"In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place," said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

items.summary:
London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds , contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions. 

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects ' design responds to the dual nature of the barn's surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

"The design centres on a dialogue between old and new. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other," studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

"The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond," he added.

"The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings."

items.title: Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen's 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler . In this interview , the Dutch designer explains why she doesn't find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

"How I think is not typical design," she told Dezeen. "So I'm never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it's just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece."

"I've never been so inspired by design in general," she added. "It's a skill that fits very well to me, but I'd rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline."

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn't have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

"I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them," she explained. "For me, it's sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be."

Tangelder is known for sculptural pieces that play with unusual material combinations. Photo by Alejandro Ramirez Orozco 

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible , as well as winning that year's Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

items.title: Harvard GSD students propose alternatives to Trump's arch
items.summary:
Landscape architecture students at Harvard's Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC , the site of US president Donald Trump 's proposed triumphal arch.

Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city's historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. 

GSD students have designed two alternative concepts for the site of Trump's proposed arch

"By recognising Memorial Circle's implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design's capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape," said Dvorak and Geitner.

The project began after Dvork and Geitner attended a seminar at the GSD taught by TCLF founding partner Charles A Birnbaum .

"As graduate students in landscape architecture, we took Birnbaum's course to ground our emerging practices in critical historical inquiry and public participation," they said.

items.title: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress
items.summary:
Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art's 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist , a graduate of the Parsons School of Design , employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

"The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I'm making," Zimbalist told Dezeen.

"Very often I favour the usage of byproducts."

The material's technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

"My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body," said Zimbalist.

"The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic."

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term "plastic".

"For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to 'biomaterials'; when people hear 'bioplastic', they tend to focus on the plastic," Zimbalist continued.

"'Biomaterial' opens up a different conversation about what the…

At 10,000 square feet, a home can easily feel more expansive than inviting. For a new residence in Dana Point, California, interior designer Lindye  Galloway approached  that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

Galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

Photography by Grace Combs

Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

Photography by Grace Combs

The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House , while lighting comes from Ravenhill , Atelier de Troupe , and Roll & Hill .

The kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area.…

items.title: “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks
items.summary:
Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne ’s public housing towers. In this interview , he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Simon Robinson (centre) is the director of Office 

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria ’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne's public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN's special rapporteur on housing , and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Flemington Estate has not yet been demolished while a class file action filed by the residents is in progress 

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office .

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility…
items.t: “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

items.title: SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration
items.summary:
Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia , USA, "breathing new life" into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

"Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station's strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop. 

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

items.title: Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen's 20x20 project in partnership with Kohler . In this interview , the New York and Paris-based designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios , 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design .

"First, it came from this game of rejection," he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

"Let's say everyone likes to use wood – I won't have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won't have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that's exactly the material I'm going to use."

"I'll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior," he continued. "I'll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture."

"You can't be safe. You always have to risk."

BIG founder Bjarke Ingels selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen's 20x20 project. Photo by Petra Kleis 

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world's best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our new series marking 20 years of Dezeen. 

Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing…

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

The White House ballroom topped out earlier this month. Above photo by Aaron Butler Jr. Top photo by Philip Yabut 

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

"This is a special structure," Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News . "It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and "selective lamination" allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

Nike has unveiled Nike Tuned Air 

"We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot," said McCartney.

"We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside."

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

items.title: The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper
items.summary:
For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

But what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style , found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper. 

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

“It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S . For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

Giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro , is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more…

items.title: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between

Though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison , an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

Tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

But her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”

That perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has…
items.t: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between

items.title: Cold Plunges Are Finding a New Place in Residential Design
items.summary:
Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a new place in residential design. As the wellness practice grows in popularity, homeowners are increasingly looking to incorporate cold therapy directly into their bathrooms, transforming what was once a standalone piece of fitness equipment into an integrated feature of the home.

The interest goes beyond athletic recovery. Cold-water immersion has been associated with potential benefits ranging from reduced muscle soreness to improved sleep and stress management, although research into its broader health effects remains limited. Still, the appeal is evident. According to Houzz’s 2024 Summer Trends Report , searches for “cold plunge” increased 74% year over year, while searches for “indoor sauna” rose 69%.

In the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging. Photography by Steve C. Wilson.

That interest reflects a larger shift toward wellness-focused residential spaces. The company’s 2026 report found that searches for “wellness room” had increased 164%, suggesting that homeowners are thinking more intentionally about how their environments can support relaxation and well-being.

For interior designers, these changing priorities are introducing new considerations into residential projects. Arizona-based designer Stephanie Larsen , who incorporates cold plunges, infrared saunas, and integrated aromatherapy systems into her work, has seen clients place…
